t: From about 1900 BCE the people of Bronze Age Crete built Europe’s first palaces, at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia: complexes of courts, storerooms and workshops that organised the island’s wealth.
Their wall paintings, carved seals, fine pottery and images of bull-leaping influenced the whole Aegean, and their ships carried their trade to Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant.
Their Linear A script is still undeciphered; after about 1450 BCE Mycenaean Greeks ruled from Knossos, and the name “Minoan” itself is modern, taken from the mythical King Minos.
dyk: Wall paintings in Minoan style have been found far from Crete, at Tel Kabri in present-day Israel and at Tell el-Dab’a, the ancient Avaris in the Nile Delta, where they include scenes of young athletes leaping over bulls.
ev: The Early Minoan period begins as Crete enters the Bronze Age
The first palaces are built at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia
The first palaces are destroyed, probably by earthquakes, and rebuilt on a grander scale
The eruption of Thera buries the town of Akrotiri under volcanic ash
Fires destroy palaces and villas across Crete; Mycenaean Greeks rule from Knossos
The palace of Knossos is finally destroyed
Cretans move to defensible heights such as Karphi as the Bronze Age ends
Arthur Evans begins to excavate the palace of Knossos

f.homeland: Crete, with settlements and strong influence on Thera, Kythera, Melos, Kea and Rhodes in the Aegean and at Miletus on the coast of Anatolia (Greece and Turkey today)
f.period: c. 3100–1100 BCE; the first palaces from c. 1900 BCE, the height of the new palaces c. 1700–1450 BCE, then Mycenaean Greek rule from Knossos and a long decline
f.known: The palaces of Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros; wall paintings and scenes of bull-leaping; Kamares ware, carved sealstones and goldwork; the undeciphered Linear A script; trade across the eastern Mediterranean
f.sources: Excavated palaces, towns, tombs and sanctuaries (Arthur Evans at Knossos from 1900, the Italian mission at Phaistos, Nikolaos Platon at Zakros, Spyridon Marinatos at Akrotiri on Thera); seals and inscriptions in scripts that cannot be read; Egyptian and Mesopotamian records; later Greek myth and writers such as Homer and Thucydides
